title: Tracker of Covered Number Ranges
statement:
Build a tracker for which parts of the number line are currently covered. Ranges are half-open: [left, right) contains every real number x with left ≤ x < right, so [1, 5) and [5, 8) touch and together cover [1, 8). Think of a video player that tracks which seconds of a clip are already buffered.

  • RangeTracker() starts with nothing covered.
  • addRange(left, right) marks all of [left, right) as covered. Parts already covered stay covered.
  • queryRange(left, right) returns true if every point of [left, right) is covered right now, otherwise false.
  • removeRange(left, right) marks all of [left, right) as not covered.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the tracker. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Removing [14, 16) splits the range into [10, 14) and [16, 20). [13, 15) hangs over the gap.
[1, 5) and [5, 8) touch, so [2, 7) is fully covered. 8 itself is not covered.

hints: Store the covered part as a sorted list of disjoint, non-touching intervals. What does each operation do to that list?
Every operation only affects intervals that overlap (or, for add, touch) [left, right). Binary search finds where that block of intervals starts and ends.

A neat encoding: keep one sorted array of boundaries, where positions 0, 2, 4, … are starts and 1, 3, 5, … are ends. The parity of a binary-search index tells you whether a point is inside a covered range.

explain.intuition:
Keep the covered set as sorted, disjoint intervals, merged whenever they touch. An add swallows every interval that overlaps or touches [left, right) and replaces them with one merged interval. A remove cuts those it overlaps, keeping at most a left stub and a right stub. A query asks whether one single interval contains the whole range; since intervals are merged, two separate intervals can never cover it together.

The boundary-array trick makes this compact. Flatten the intervals into one sorted array b = [s0, e0, s1, e1, …]. For a point x, the number of boundaries ≤ x is odd exactly when x is covered. An add or remove replaces the slice of boundaries between left and right with at most two new boundaries, chosen by the parity of the slice ends. Binary search finds the slice; the splice costs O(k) for k removed boundaries.
steps: Keep a sorted array b of boundaries; covered ranges are [b[0], b[1]), [b[2], b[3]), …
addRange: i = first index with b[i] ≥ left, j = first index with b[j] > right. Replace b[i … j − 1] with left if i is even, then right if j is even.
removeRange: same i and j, but keep left if i is odd and right if j is odd (they become an end and a start).
queryRange: i = first index with b[i] > left, j = first index with b[j] ≥ right. Covered iff i === j and i is odd: one interval starts at or before left and ends at or after right.
pitfalls: Treating ranges as closed. [1, 2) and [3, 4) leave [2, 3) uncovered, while [1, 5) and [5, 8) leave no gap.
Storing every covered integer in a set. Coordinates go up to 10⁹.
Not merging touching intervals on add. Then a query spanning the joint is answered with "not covered".

complexity.time: O(log n + k) per call, k = boundaries removed

solutions.title: Sorted interval list, rebuilt per call
solutions.idea: Walk the list of disjoint intervals and build the new list: merge on add, cut on remove, binary search on query.
solutions.time: O(n) per add/remove, O(log n) per query

solutions.title: Boundary array with parity
solutions.idea: One sorted array of starts and ends; binary search locates the affected slice and its parity says which new boundaries to keep.

followups: Add coveredLength() returning the total covered length. How do you keep it up to date in O(1) per change?
With 10⁶ calls the splice cost can add up. How would a balanced tree or a segment tree with lazy assignment help?
